description_full: NRC Health provides analytics and insights to measure and improve patient and employee experience for healthcare organizations in the United States. The company offers market experience solutions, a subscription-based services for improved tracking of awareness, perception, and consistency of healthcare brands; assessment of differentiators; and segmentation tools to evaluate the needs, wants, and behaviors of communities through assessments. It also provides patient experience solutions, a cross-continuum multi-mode digital platform that collects and measures data to improve patient experience, engagement, and loyalty; employee experience solutions, which combines health care with technology comprising engagement, pulse, lifecycle, culture of safety, and magnet RN satisfaction; and consumer experience solution that offers online reputation solutions, community insights, and cross-journey listening through nGage. In addition, the company offers Huey, an AI engine built for Human Understanding that serves as a healthcare experience management companion; and governance solutions provided through national conferences, publications, advisory services, and an online portal for not-for-profit health system boards of directors, executives, and physician leadership. Further, it provides patient experience, service recovery, care transitions, employee engagement, reputation management, rounding, and brand loyalty. The company was formerly known as National Research Corporation and changed its name to NRC Health April 2026. The company was founded in 1981 and is headquartered in Lincoln, Nebraska.

financial_summary: NRC Health is a small-cap healthcare business with a $564M market cap on $137M of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at -3% over the past three years and +3% annually across the full decade, and a shrinking top line is the hardest headwind any business can overcome.
Returns on capital run at 42% against a 8% cost of capital — a 34-point spread that is the clearest signature of an economic moat.

The business throws off $16M in free cash flow — roughly 11 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 2.34× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, debt is moderate at 2.3× net debt/EBITDA, serviceable in normal conditions but worth watching through a downturn, and interest coverage runs at 4.7×.

Management returns a meaningful 5.5% of market cap to owners through dividends and buybacks, a strong signal of disciplined capital allocation, and insiders hold 51% of the shares, so management thinks like owners because it is one — the strongest alignment there is, and within its sector the business captures 1.9× its fair share of profits, a structural advantage visible in the numbers.

Payout ratio looks stretched — the dividend’s own margin of safety is thin

Patent cliffs, drug-pricing reform, and reimbursement pressure — a single regulatory change can reset the pricing power that justifies the multiple.
Clinical trial concentration risk — binary FDA outcomes on a lead asset can wipe out billions in market cap in a single session.
GLP-1 disruption across sub-sectors — weight-loss drugs are reshaping demand for orthopaedics, cardiovascular devices, and sleep-apnea treatments in ways not yet priced in.

11 consecutive years of dividend payments — an operating record that makes the dividend claim credible
ROIC sits in the top quartile of Healthcare peers — the moat is wider than the neighbourhood
Healthcare sector showing strong relative momentum, outperforming the market by 13% over 3 months
Healthcare ETF in a sustained uptrend above its long-term average

sect: Its 16% operating margin runs 17pp above the Healthcare median (0%), a real cost or pricing edge over peers.
It captures 1.88x its revenue share in sector profits, taking a disproportionate slice of the profit pool.
Over five years it has been losing share of the sector profit pool (-18.0% a year).
The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.05 across 462 companies in the universe; the top four hold 35% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares are in a strong uptrend, up 34% over the past year excluding the latest month.
The price sits near the top of its 52-week range, 4% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 58% and a beta of 0.70, it is more defensive than the market, though its beta has shifted (1y -0.26 vs 5y 0.51), so read it loosely.
About $2.3M trades a day, enough to build a position.
In past sell-offs it fell 50% in the 2020 crash and 24% in the 2022 bear market.
val: The price sits above its DCF fair value of $22.23 (margin of safety -19%), so there is no valuation cushion.
The fair-value models disagree (dispersion 28%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $16.34 to $30.72 (P10-P90), so treat the estimate as noisy.
On multiples it looks expensive against Healthcare peers: P/E 98.4 vs 26.2, EV/EBITDA 24.0 vs 15.5 and P/FCF 35.8 vs 23.8 (sector median).
Against its own history it is dear: the EBIT multiple sits 41% above its 10-year median.
Earnings yields are thin: an FCF yield of 2.8% (below the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 3.4% (vs the 8% bar).
The Street target $27.00 on average, 2% above the price.
prof: ROIC of 42% clears the cost of capital of 8.0% by 34pp, the mark of a value creator; returns have swung a lot from year to year (CV 0.43).
It converts 11% of revenue into free cash flow.
Earnings quality looks solid: cash conversion of 2.34x.
ROE of 81% is amplified by 9.6x balance-sheet leverage (DuPont), so ROIC is the cleaner read on the business.
It spends 2.4% of revenue on stock compensation (above the 2% gate).
hlth: Leverage is moderate at 2.3x net debt to EBITDA ($4.1M of cash against $75.0M of debt), above the 1.5x gate, with interest covered 4.7x.
The current ratio of 0.55 means short-term liabilities exceed current assets.
Goodwill makes up 49% of assets, a soft asset exposed to impairment.
growth: Revenue has compounded at -3.2% over 3 years, 0.6% over 5 years and 3.0% over 10 years, so growth is decelerating.
At current returns, reinvesting 20% of profits supports about 8.3% a year of fundamental growth, enough to sustain growth.
Free cash flow has compounded -15.5% a year over five years, short of the 5% durability bar.
Forward indicators: a backlog worth 1% of annual revenue.
Capex roughly matches depreciation (1.4x, 7.8% of sales), a maintenance pace.
Its Rule of 40 score is 10, below the 40 that marks a healthy growth business.
own: Insiders own 51.2%, meaningful skin in the game, and institutions hold 53%.
Insiders have only bought over the past year (1 purchase).
It returns 5.5% a year to shareholders (3.6% in buybacks and 2.4% in dividends).
The share count has shrunk 3.5% a year over five years, steadily raising each holder's stake.
It pays out 237% of earnings, more than it earns, so the dividend is at risk.
Short interest is elevated at 45.5% of the float, 7.1 days to cover.
people: With about 357 employees, each generates about $385K of revenue, in line with the Healthcare median, and revenue has grown 4.3% a year across its filed history.
That works out to $44K of free cash flow per employee.
CEO pay is $5.7M (15x revenue per employee), and compensation governance scores poorly (10/10, lower is better).
